analysis.one_liner: Requires large companies to test and report the harms of the software they use to make high-stakes decisions about people.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing, markup, or vote in the House Energy and Commerce Committee before the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have directed the Federal Trade Commission to write rules requiring large companies to assess their automated decision systems — the software that screens job applicants, sets credit terms, prices insurance, and makes similar high-stakes calls. Companies would have to test whether these systems perform differently by race, sex, age, or disability, document how consumers can contest decisions, and file annual reports, with key information posted in a public FTC database. The bill was referred to a House committee and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers whose access to jobs, housing, credit, healthcare, education, and utilities is decided by software would gain [S2]. The bill would have required the companies behind those systems to study and document whether their systems perform differently by race, sex, age, disability, and other characteristics, disclose how consumers can contest or appeal decisions, and register key details in a public, searchable FTC repository [S2]. State attorneys general could also sue on residents' behalf [S2].

how_it_helps.text: Requires large companies to perform and document ongoing impact assessments of automated systems used in 'critical decisions' — employment, housing, credit, healthcare, education, utilities, and more — before and after deployment [S2].
Mandates testing for differential performance by race, sex, age, disability, and other characteristics, including how such characteristics were inferred from data such as ZIP codes [S2].
Requires companies to try to eliminate or mitigate negative impacts, and to document which harms they left unaddressed and why [S2].
Creates a public, searchable FTC repository telling consumers which companies use these systems, what decisions they make, and how to contest or appeal a decision [S2].
Lets state attorneys general sue on behalf of residents and gives the FTC full Federal Trade Commission Act enforcement powers [S2].

analysis.who_pays: If it passed, the cost would fall on large companies that use automated decision systems in areas like hiring, lending, housing, and healthcare, which would have to perform and document ongoing impact assessments, consult outside stakeholders, and file annual summary reports to the FTC [S2]. The FTC's new Bureau of Technology (at least 50 staff) and 25 additional enforcement staff would also be funded by appropriations, i.e. taxpayers [S2]. Some compliance costs could be passed on to consumers through higher prices [S2].
analysis.who_pays_short: Large algorithm-using companies and the FTC

drawbacks.text: Impact assessments themselves stay confidential: nothing in the bill requires companies to disclose their assessments to the Commission or the public beyond the narrower annual summary reports [S2].
Consumers get no private right of action — only the FTC and state attorneys general can enforce the law, so individuals harmed by a biased algorithm cannot sue directly under it [S2].

Compliance would have been costly for covered companies, and some costs could flow to consumers through higher prices; the bill itself instructs the FTC to weigh 'the administrative burden placed on the Commission and the covered entity' when writing rules [S2].
The rules would not have taken effect quickly: the FTC had two years to write regulations, and the regulations' requirements would take effect two years after that [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main benefit — forcing companies to find and disclose bias in the software that decides who gets hired, housed, and lent to — addresses a real and growing gap, since consumers usually cannot even know an algorithm made the decision, let alone contest it. The costs fall on large companies, which have the resources to comply, and the bill exempts smaller firms. The design has real limits, though: the full assessments stay private, only the FTC and state attorneys general can sue, and the rules would not have taken effect for roughly four years after enactment. On balance it is a modest, targeted transparency measure whose cost is small relative to its public benefit — and it never got the chance to be tested, because it died without a single hearing or vote.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to a House committee and its Innovation, Data, and Commerce subcommittee the day after introduction, and sat there with no hearing or vote until the 118th Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on September 21, 2023, and referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce [S1] [S4].
The next day it was referred to the Subcommittee on Innovation, Data, and Commerce [S4].
No further action appears in the record: no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor vote occurred before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S4].
All 15 cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican signed on [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The companies that use algorithmic systems in hiring, lending, housing, and healthcare decisions are better off, because the assessment, testing, and public disclosure requirements were never imposed. Consumers gained nothing from the bill's failure.

for.name: Rep. Yvette D. Clarke of New York
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 14 Democratic colleagues to cosponsor it

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee leadership
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or floor action on the bill; it remained in committee until the Congress ended

sides.party_line_note: All 15 cosponsors were House Democrats, and the bill sat in a Republican-controlled committee until the Congress ended, so support was one-sided from the start.

industries.note: These companies would have faced new testing, documentation, consultation, and annual reporting duties for systems used in hiring, lending, housing, and healthcare, plus public disclosure of how consumers can contest decisions. The bill's failure means these obligations never took effect.

industries.industry: Data-driven finance, insurance, and platform companies
industries.note: The bill reaches any large company deploying automated decision systems in critical decisions, including financial firms and online rental and lodging platforms, requiring performance and bias testing and public filing of summary reports.

industries.industry: State attorneys general and state consumer-protection authority
industries.note: The bill would not have preempted state, tribal, or local laws, leaving state-level AI and privacy rules fully intact.
